Many values never change once they are set: a person’s date of birth, the value of pi, the address of an API. Dart gives you two keywords to say so, and the compiler then stops anyone from changing them by accident.

final: set once, at run time

A final variable can be assigned exactly one time. The value can be worked out while the program runs.

void main() {
 final name = 'Sita';
 final startedAt = DateTime.now(); // known only at run time

 // name = 'Gita'; // error: a final variable can only be set once
 print('$name started at ${startedAt.year}');
}

const: fixed at compile time

A const value must be known before the program runs. It is baked into the compiled program.

item.title: Inheritance in Dart: extends, super and @override
item.description:
Inheritance lets one class build on another. The new class (the subclass or child) gets all the fields and methods of the existing one (the superclass or parent), and can add or change behaviour.

It models an “is a” relationship: a dog is an animal, a manager is an employee.

extends

class Animal {
 String name;
 Animal(this.name);

 void eat() => print('$name is eating');
 void sleep() => print('$name is sleeping');
}

class Dog extends Animal {
 Dog(super.name);

 void bark() => print('$name says Woof!');
}

void main() {
 var dog = Dog('Bruno');
 dog.eat(); // inherited
 dog.sleep(); // inherited
 dog.bark(); // its own
}

Bruno is eating
Bruno is sleeping
Bruno says Woof!

Dog did not define eat, sleep or name. It inherited them.

item.title: where, map, reduce and fold in Dart: Filter and Transform Collections
item.description:
Most loops do one of three things: pick some items, change every item, or boil everything down to one value. Dart has a method for each, and using them makes the intent of your code obvious.

where: keep the items that pass a test

void main() {
 var ages = [12, 25, 17, 40, 8, 33];

 var adults = ages.where((age) => age >= 18).toList();
 print(adults);
}

[25, 40, 33]

The function you pass is called once per item and returns true to keep it. where never changes the original list.

item.title: Abstract Classes and Methods in Dart
item.description:
An abstract class is a class that is incomplete on purpose. You cannot create an object of it directly. It exists to be extended, and it can declare methods that subclasses must provide.

The problem

What should area() return for a generic Shape? There is no sensible answer. Returning 0 is a lie, and nothing stops a subclass from forgetting to override it.

Abstract methods

An abstract method has a signature but no body. It ends with a semicolon.

item.title: The Dart Event Loop: Microtasks and Events Explained
item.description:
Dart runs your code on a single thread, yet it handles taps, timers and network responses without getting stuck. The mechanism behind this is the event loop. Knowing how it works explains the order in which asynchronous code runs, and why an app can freeze.

One thread, two queues

Dart keeps two queues of work waiting to run:

  • The event queue holds things from the outside world: timers, I/O results, user input, messages from isolates, and callbacks from Future(...) and Future.delayed(...).
  • The microtask queue holds very short internal jobs that must run as soon as possible: completions of already-finished futures, and anything scheduled with scheduleMicrotask or Future.microtask.

The loop

  1. Run main() from start to finish. All synchronous code runs first.
  2. Run every microtask, until the microtask queue is empty.
  3. Take one event from the event queue and run its handler.
  4. Go back to step 2.
  5. When both queues are empty and nothing is pending, the program ends.

The key rule: microtasks always run before the next event.

item.title: Spread Operator, Collection if and Collection for in Dart
item.description:
Dart lets you put a little logic directly inside a collection literal. These three features are small, but they are used on almost every screen of a Flutter app.

The spread operator

... unpacks one collection into another.

void main() {
 var fruits = ['apple', 'banana'];
 var vegetables = ['carrot', 'spinach'];

 var basket = ['bread', ...fruits, ...vegetables, 'milk'];
 print(basket);
}

[bread, apple, banana, carrot, spinach, milk]

Without the dots you would get a list inside a list.

It is also the simplest way to copy a list.

item.title: Type Conversion in Dart: Converting Between Types
item.description:
Dart never converts types behind your back. '5' + 3 is an error, not 8 or '53'. When you need a different type, you ask for it.

String to number

void main() {
 var a = int.parse('25');
 var b = double.parse('9.75');

 print(a + 5);
 print(b + 0.25);
}

30
10.0

parse throws a FormatException when the text is not a valid number. For input you do not control, use tryParse, which returns null on failure.

void main() {
 var input = '12abc';
 var number = int.tryParse(input);

 if (number == null) {
 print('"$input" is not a whole number');
 } else {
 print(number * 2);
 }

 // Provide a fallback in one line.
 print(int.tryParse('oops') ?? 0);
}

"12abc" is not a whole number
0

Number to string

void main() {
 var n = 42;
 var price = 1234.5678;

 print(n.toString() + '!');
 print('$n!'); // interpolation converts for you
 print(price.toStringAsFixed(2));
 print(255.toRadixString(16)); // hexadecimal
 print(5.toString().padLeft(2, '0'));
}

42!
42!
1234.57
ff
05

int and double

void main() {
 print(7.toDouble());
 print(7.9.toInt()); // drops the fraction
 print(7.9.round()); // nearest
 print(7.1.ceil());
 print(7.9.floor());
}

7.0
7
8
8
7

String to bool

There is no built-in conversion that guesses. Compare the text yourself, or use bool.tryParse, which accepts 'true' and 'false'.

item.title: Interfaces in Dart: The implements Keyword
item.description:
An interface is a list of things a class promises it can do, without saying how. Other code can then depend on the promise and not on any particular class.

Dart takes an unusual approach: every class automatically defines an interface made of all its public members. Any other class can implement it.

implements

A class that implements an interface must provide every member itself. It inherits nothing.

abstract class Printer {
 void printDocument(String text);
}

class LaserPrinter implements Printer {
 @override
 void printDocument(String text) => print('Laser printing: $text');
}

class PdfPrinter implements Printer {
 @override
 void printDocument(String text) => print('Saving "$text" as PDF');
}

void sendToPrinter(Printer printer) {
 printer.printDocument('Invoice #42');
}

void main() {
 sendToPrinter(LaserPrinter());
 sendToPrinter(PdfPrinter());
}

Laser printing: Invoice #42
Saving "Invoice #42" as PDF

sendToPrinter works with anything that implements Printer, including classes written years later.

item.title: Isolates in Dart: Running Code in Parallel
item.description:
async and await let Dart do other things while it waits. They do not help when the processor itself is busy, for example parsing a 50 MB JSON file or applying a filter to a photo. That work blocks the single thread and freezes the app.

The answer is an isolate: a separate worker with its own thread, its own memory and its own event loop.

Isolates are not available on the web, so these examples will not run in DartPad. Run them with dart run.

item.title: Queue in Dart: Adding and Removing from Both Ends
item.description:
A Queue is a collection built for adding and removing items at both ends. Removing the first item of a List is slow because every other item has to shift down. A queue does it instantly.

Queue lives in the dart:collection library, so it needs an import.

Creating a queue

import 'dart:collection';

void main() {
 var queue = Queue<String>();

 queue.add('Asha'); // same as addLast
 queue.addLast('Bimal');
 queue.addFirst('Chandra');

 print(queue);
 print(queue.first);
 print(queue.last);
 print(queue.length);
}

{Chandra, Asha, Bimal}
Chandra
Bimal
3

Removing from either end

import 'dart:collection';

void main() {
 var queue = Queue.of([10, 20, 30, 40]);

 print(queue.removeFirst());
 print(queue.removeLast());
 print(queue);
}

10
40
{20, 30}

Both methods throw a StateError on an empty queue, so check isNotEmpty first.

item.title: Reading User Input in Dart with stdin
item.description:
So far your programs have only talked. To listen, a console program reads from standard input using the dart:io library.

dart:io does not work in DartPad or in the browser. Save these examples to a file and run them with dart run file.dart.

Reading a line of text

import 'dart:io';

void main() {
 stdout.write('What is your name? ');
 String? name = stdin.readLineSync();

 print('Nice to meet you, $name!');
}

What is your name? Priya
Nice to meet you, Priya!

Two things to notice:

item.title: Generators in Dart: sync*, async*, yield and yield*
item.description:
A generator is a function that produces a sequence of values one at a time, on demand. It pauses after each value and resumes when the next is requested. Dart has two kinds:

Keyword Returns Values arrive
sync* Iterable<T> Immediately, when asked
async* Stream<T> Over time

In both, yield hands out one value.

A synchronous generator

Iterable<int> countTo(int max) sync* {
 for (var i = 1; i <= max; i++) {
 yield i;
 }
}

void main() {
 for (final n in countTo(4)) {
 print(n);
 }
 print(countTo(3).toList());
}

1
2
3
4
[1, 2, 3]

Generators are lazy

The body runs only as far as needed to produce the value being asked for.

item.title: Mixins in Dart: Reusing Code with the with Keyword
item.description:
Inheritance lets a class take code from one parent. But some abilities cut across family trees: both a Duck and an Aeroplane can fly, yet they share no sensible parent. A mixin is a bundle of fields and methods that can be added to any class.

Defining and using a mixin

mixin Flyer {
 void fly() => print('$runtimeType is flying');
}

mixin Swimmer {
 void swim() => print('$runtimeType is swimming');
}

class Animal {}

class Duck extends Animal with Flyer, Swimmer {}

class Fish extends Animal with Swimmer {}

class Aeroplane with Flyer {}

void main() {
 Duck()
 ..fly()
 ..swim();
 Fish().swim();
 Aeroplane().fly();
}

Duck is flying
Duck is swimming
Fish is swimming
Aeroplane is flying

A class can use many mixins, listed after with. Unlike implements, you get the working code.

item.title: Collection Performance in Dart: Choosing the Fastest Structure
item.description:
For a handful of items, every collection is fast. Once you have thousands, the choice of collection and method decides whether your app feels instant or sluggish.

The cost of common operations

“Constant” means the time does not grow with the size of the collection. “Linear” means that with twice the items it takes twice as long.

Operation List Set Map
Read by index or key Constant n/a Constant
Add at the end Constant Constant Constant
Insert or remove at the start Linear n/a n/a
contains / containsKey Linear Constant Constant
Remove by value or key Linear Constant Constant

Use a Set or Map for lookups

This is the improvement that matters most in practice.

item.title: Best Practices for Asynchronous Programming in Dart
item.description:
You now know the tools. This lesson collects the habits that separate async code that works on a good day from async code that works always.

1. Prefer async and await to then

await keeps code flat and lets you use ordinary try/catch, loops and if.

Future<int> fetchA() async => 2;
Future<int> fetchB(int a) async => a * 10;

// Harder to read and to extend.
Future<int> withThen() => fetchA().then((a) => fetchB(a)).then((b) => b + 1);

// Clear.
Future<int> withAwait() async {
 final a = await fetchA();
 final b = await fetchB(a);
 return b + 1;
}

Future<void> main() async {
 print(await withThen());
 print(await withAwait());
}

21
21

2. Never use async void

A function declared void f() async cannot be awaited, and its errors cannot be caught by the caller. Return Future<void>.

item.title: Polymorphism in Dart: One Interface, Many Forms
item.description:
Polymorphism means “many forms”. In code, it means you can call the same method on different kinds of objects, and each one responds in its own way. The calling code does not need to know which kind it has.

The idea in one example

abstract class Notification {
 void send(String message);
}

class EmailNotification extends Notification {
 @override
 void send(String message) => print('Email: $message');
}

class SmsNotification extends Notification {
 @override
 void send(String message) => print('SMS: $message');
}

class PushNotification extends Notification {
 @override
 void send(String message) => print('Push: $message');
}

void main() {
 List<Notification> channels = [
 EmailNotification(),
 SmsNotification(),
 PushNotification(),
 ];

 for (final channel in channels) {
 channel.send('Your order has shipped');
 }
}

Email: Your order has shipped
SMS: Your order has shipped
Push: Your order has shipped

The loop contains no if and no knowledge of email or SMS. Adding a WhatsAppNotification class later needs no change to the loop. That is the payoff.

item.title: Enums in Dart: Simple and Enhanced Enumerations
item.description:
An enum (enumeration) is a type with a small, fixed set of possible values. Use one whenever a variable should only ever be one of a few named options: the days of the week, the state of an order, the size of a T-shirt.

Why not strings?

With String status = 'shiped'; the typo compiles and fails silently. With an enum, a misspelt value is a compile error and autocomplete lists every option.

item.title: Extension Methods in Dart
item.description:
An extension adds new methods, getters and operators to a type you did not write and cannot change, such as String, int or List. The new members then look and feel as if they had always been there.

Without and with an extension

Without one, you write a helper function and the call reads inside out:

capitalize(name.trim())

With one, it chains naturally:

extension StringExtras on String {
 String capitalize() {
 if (isEmpty) return this;
 return '${this[0].toUpperCase()}${substring(1)}';
 }

 bool get isBlank => trim().isEmpty;
}

void main() {
 print('dart'.capitalize());
 print(' hello '.trim().capitalize());
 print(' '.isBlank);
}

Dart
Hello
true

Inside the extension, this is the value the method was called on. Members of that value, like isEmpty and substring, can be used directly.

item.title: Extension Types in Dart: Zero-Cost Wrappers
item.description:
Imagine a function transfer(int fromAccount, int toAccount, int amount). All three are int, so passing them in the wrong order compiles happily and moves money to the wrong place.

An extension type fixes this. It wraps an existing type in a new, separate type that the compiler tells apart, and it costs nothing at run time because the wrapper is erased when the program is compiled.

Declaring an extension type

extension type AccountId(int value) {}
extension type Rupees(int value) {}

void transfer(AccountId from, AccountId to, Rupees amount) {
 print('Moving ${amount.value} from ${from.value} to ${to.value}');
}

void main() {
 var mine = AccountId(1001);
 var yours = AccountId(2002);
 var amount = Rupees(500);

 transfer(mine, yours, amount);
 // transfer(mine, amount, yours); // error: Rupees is not an AccountId
 // transfer(1001, 2002, 500); // error: int is not an AccountId
}

Moving 500 from 1001 to 2002

AccountId(int value) declares both the constructor and the representation: the underlying value, available as .value.

item.title: Generics in Dart: Type-Safe Reusable Code
item.description:
You have been using generics since the collections chapter. In List<String>, the <String> is a type argument: it tells the list what it holds. Generics let you write a class or function once and use it safely with many types.

The problem generics solve

class IntBox {
 final int value;
 IntBox(this.value);
}

class StringBox {
 final String value;
 StringBox(this.value);
}
// ...and another class for every type?

You could use Object or dynamic to hold anything, but then you lose type checking and have to cast everywhere.

item.title: Object Equality in Dart: ==, hashCode and identical
item.description:
Are two objects “the same”? There are two different questions hiding in that word:

  • Identity: are they the very same object in memory?
  • Equality: do they represent the same value?

The default is identity

For your own classes, == compares identity unless you say otherwise.

class Point {
 final int x, y;
 Point(this.x, this.y);
}

void main() {
 var a = Point(1, 2);
 var b = Point(1, 2);
 var c = a;

 print(a == b); // different objects
 print(a == c); // same object
 print(identical(a, c));
}

false
true
true

Two points with the same coordinates are not equal. That is rarely what you want for data classes.

item.title: Class Modifiers in Dart 3: base, interface, final, sealed and mixin
item.description:
By default a Dart class is wide open: anyone can construct it, extend it, and implement its interface. Class modifiers, added in Dart 3, let the author of a class restrict that. They are most useful when you publish a package and want to control how other people build on your types.

The three things you can do with a class

Action Meaning
Construct Create an instance: Vehicle()
Extend Inherit its code: class Car extends Vehicle
Implement Copy its shape only: class Fake implements Vehicle

What each modifier allows

item.title: Operator Overloading and Callable Classes in Dart
item.description:
Operators such as +, < and [] are just methods with special names. Dart lets you define them for your own classes, so that objects representing numbers, vectors, money or collections can be used with natural syntax.

Defining an operator

Use the operator keyword followed by the symbol.

class Vector {
 final double x, y;
 const Vector(this.x, this.y);

 Vector operator +(Vector other) => Vector(x + other.x, y + other.y);
 Vector operator -(Vector other) => Vector(x - other.x, y - other.y);
 Vector operator *(double factor) => Vector(x * factor, y * factor);
 Vector operator -() => Vector(-x, -y); // unary minus

 @override
 String toString() => 'Vector($x, $y)';
}

void main() {
 const a = Vector(1, 2);
 const b = Vector(3, 4);

 print(a + b);
 print(b - a);
 print(a * 3);
 print(-a);
}

Vector(4.0, 6.0)
Vector(2.0, 2.0)
Vector(3.0, 6.0)
Vector(-1.0, -2.0)

a + b is exactly the same as calling a method named + on a with the argument b.

item.title: Immutable Classes and copyWith in Dart
item.description:
An immutable object cannot change after it is created. To “change” it, you make a new object with the new values. This sounds wasteful, but it makes code much easier to reason about, and it is how state works in Flutter, Riverpod and Bloc.

The problem with mutable objects

class Cart {
 List<String> items;
 Cart(this.items);
}

void main() {
 final saved = Cart(['apple']);
 final current = saved; // the same object, not a copy

 current.items.add('mango');
 print(saved.items); // the "saved" cart changed too!
}

[apple, mango]

Two variables pointed at one object, so a change through one was visible through the other. Bugs like this are hard to find in a big app.
